fields.description: Why does Jesus tell us to keep asking? Here is what the Bible teaches about persistent, persevering prayer — why it matters, what it accomplishes, and how to keep praying when heaven seems silent.
fields.body_html:
Almost every Christian has faced the same quiet discouragement: you pray for something — earnestly, sincerely — and nothing seems to happen. The temptation, then, is to conclude that prayer does not work, or that God is not listening, and to give up. Yet Jesus, who knew this temptation would come, taught his disciples the exact opposite. He told them “that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). Persistence in prayer is not a sign of weak faith or of nagging an unwilling God; it is one of the great secrets of the praying life, and Scripture is full of its power. Here is what the Bible teaches about persistent prayer — and why it is worth everything to learn it.

Jesus commands us to keep asking

Our Lord could not have been plainer. “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7). In the original, those verbs carry the sense of continuing action: keep on asking, keep on seeking, keep on knocking. Prayer, for Jesus, is not a single request dropped into a slot but a persevering pursuit. He drove the point home with two memorable parables. In one, a man wakes his friend at midnight for bread and is answered “because of his impudence” — his shameless persistence (Luke 11:8). In the other, a widow wins justice from an unjust judge simply because she will not stop coming (Luke 18:4–5). The lesson is not that God is reluctant like that judge, but the reverse: if even a corrupt judge yields to persistence, how much more will a loving Father answer his children who cry to him day and night? “And will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night?” (Luke 18:7).

Persistence is not about changing God’s mind

Why, though, must we keep asking? Does God need to be worn down? Not at all — he already knows what we need before we ask (Matthew 6:8). Persistent prayer is not for God’s sake but for ours. It is one of the chief means by which God grows our faith, purifies our desires, and deepens our dependence on him. A prayer we abandon at the first delay was never very serious; a prayer we carry for months and years becomes the very shape of our walk with God. Persistence sifts our motives — we stop asking for what we do not truly want — and it teaches us to want God himself more than his gifts. The delay, far from being God’s indifference, is often his workshop, where he is doing something deeper in us than the answer itself would accomplish. E. M. Bounds, whose life was steeped in this kind of praying, saw the whole world as shaped by it:

God shapes the world by prayer. The more praying there is in the world the better the world will be, the mightier the forces against evil.E. M. Bounds

The saints prayed with holy stubbornness

Scripture’s great pray-ers were persistent to the point of holy boldness. Jacob wrestled through the night and would not let go: “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Genesis 32:26). Elijah prayed for rain and sent his servant to look seven times, praying again after each empty report, until at last a cloud appeared (1 Kings 18:43–44). Daniel prayed for twenty-one days, not knowing that the answer had been dispatched from the first day and delayed only by unseen opposition (Daniel 10:12–13). The early church, when Peter was imprisoned, was “earnestly praying to God for him” (Acts 12:5) — and God opened the prison. These were not people who prayed once and shrugged; they laid hold of God and would not let go. This is the “prevailing prayer” that Dwight L. Moody urged on believers — prayer that keeps its grip until the answer comes.

Why heaven is sometimes silent

Still, the honest question remains: what about the prayers that seem to go unanswered? Scripture gives us several truths to steady us here. Sometimes the answer is not yet — God’s timing is not ours, and “with the Lord one day is as a thousand years” (2 Peter 3:8). Sometimes the answer is no, because we “ask wrongly, to spend it on our passions” (James 4:3), and a good Father will not give a harmful thing however earnestly we beg. And sometimes God is giving something better than we asked — Paul pleaded three times for his thorn to be removed, and instead received grace sufficient to bear it, which was the greater gift (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Persistent prayer is not a technique for forcing God’s hand; it is a relationship of trust in which we keep bringing our requests while leaving the outcome to a wisdom higher than ours. The persevering pray-er learns to say, with each petition, “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42) — and to trust that a delayed or redirected answer is still the answer of a Father who cannot fail to love his child.

What persistence works in us

It is worth dwelling on the hidden work that persistent prayer does in the one who prays, because this is often the real reason God asks us to keep asking. A prayer quickly answered leaves us much as it found us; a prayer we must carry for years reshapes us from the inside. As we keep bringing the same request, God gently exposes our motives — are we seeking his glory or merely our own comfort? He deepens our desire, so that what began as a passing wish becomes a settled longing. He teaches us patience, that rare fruit that grows only in the soil of waiting. And above all he draws us closer to himself, for the one who prays long learns to love the Giver more than the gift. Hannah wept and prayed for years before Samuel was born, and by the time the answer came she was ready to give the child right back to God (1 Samuel 1:27–28) — the long waiting had done its work in her heart. This is why we must never measure the worth of our praying by how quickly it is answered. The delay is not wasted time; it is the very season in which God is doing his deepest work, both in the situation we are praying about and, more importantly, in us. “Wait for the Lord; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the Lord!” (Psalm 27:14). The waiting itself, endured in faith, is part of the answer.

There is also a strange dignity that God grants us in persistent prayer: he lets our prayers genuinely matter. Scripture presents prayer not as a formality but as a real means by which God accomplishes his purposes in the world — “The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working” (James 5:16). When we persevere, we are not performing a religious exercise; we are taking up the astonishing invitation to work together with God, our small persistent faith becoming, in his hands, part of how his kingdom comes.

How to keep praying when you want to quit

How, then, do we persevere when we are tempted to give up? First, we remember Jesus’ command and take it as a promise: he told us to keep asking precisely because it is worth continuing. Second, we pray from God’s promises, not merely our feelings — anchoring our requests in what he has said, for “this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14). Third, we enlist others, as the church did for Peter, for there is strength in shared, persistent intercession. Fourth, we watch for God’s smaller answers along the way, which encourage us to keep asking for the larger ones. And above all, we keep our eyes on the God to whom we pray rather than on the delay, refusing to measure his love by the speed of his replies. “Let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9).

Persistent prayer, in the end, is simply the refusal to stop trusting God. It is faith that has learned patience, love that will not let go, hope that keeps knocking at a door it is sure will open. It is the widow at the judge’s gate, Jacob at the ford, Elijah on the mountain, the church at the prison — and it is you, on your knees, bringing the same request to your Father yet again, believing that he hears, that he cares, and that in his perfect time he will answer. “Continue steadfastly in prayer” (Colossians 4:2). Of all the habits a Christian can form, few will do more to deepen your soul and change your world than this one: to pray, and not give up.
